blocks.html: Mirsad Cerimovic, CAM, CMCA, AMS · March 14, 2023 · 6 min read

Most condo associations do not fail because of money, weather, or a single bad decision. They fail slowly, through a breakdown in how the board works. When a board loses the confidence of the owners it serves, every meeting becomes a battle, good volunteers walk away, and the association drifts. The encouraging news: the root cause is well understood, and it is fixable.
The #1 Reason: Treating the Board as a Throne, Not a Trust

The single most common reason condo boards fail is a breakdown of trust — and that breakdown almost always begins when a board stops acting as a fiduciary body serving every owner and starts operating as a personal platform. A board is a trust. Members are legally obligated to act in the best interest of the whole community, not a faction, not a friendship, and not a grudge. The moment owners sense the board is opaque, arbitrary, or self-serving, cooperation collapses and conflict takes its place.
The Warning Signs of a Failing Board

items: Lack of transparency. Decisions are made with no explanation, minutes are thin or missing, and owners learn about major changes after the fact.
Micromanagement. The board insists on doing the manager's job, second-guesses every vendor, and bottlenecks routine work.
Favoritism. Rules are enforced strictly for some owners and quietly ignored for others.
Poor communication. Owners feel unheard, so they stop engaging — until they are angry enough to litigate.
Volunteer burnout. The same one or two people carry everything until they quit, leaving a vacuum.
Misunderstanding fiduciary duty. Members vote based on personal preference rather than the association's documents and best interest.

blocks.html: How to Fix a Struggling Board
Rebuilding a board starts with rebuilding trust, and trust is built through consistent, visible behavior:

items: Communicate first. Publish agendas and minutes, explain the reasoning behind decisions, and tell owners about problems before the rumor mill does.
Enforce rules uniformly. Apply the same standard to every owner, every time — including board members.
Separate governance from operations. Let the board set direction and let a manager execute it.
Invest in education. New board members should understand fiduciary duty, the governing documents, and the budget from day one.
Share the load. Use committees and professional support so no single volunteer burns out.

blocks.html: Also useful: A new board member’s first 30 days; keeping board decisions from getting lost.

Strong boards are not the ones that never disagree — they are the ones that disagree in a structured, transparent process that owners can see and respect.
